title: How To Get Students To Follow Directions
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin diagnoses a familiar frustration — students who mentally check out before directions are finished, then ask questions already answered — as a directions-giving problem rather than a listening problem. He offers a nine-step sequence for delivering directions effectively: securing full attention and pausing before speaking, announcing that directions aren't finished, breaking instructions into discrete steps, posting multi-step directions visually, modeling each step in detail, answering clarifying questions, checking for understanding before releasing students, pausing again for effect, and finally giving a clear 'go' signal. He stresses that once these steps are followed, any breakdown becomes an execution problem belonging to students, not a case for repeating instructions; instead, the 'do it again' strategy should be used. The piece frames rigorous, methodical direction-giving as the fix for a problem many teachers wrongly attribute to student inattention alone.
points: Students who seem inattentive during directions are often reacting to directions that are poorly sequenced, not simply being disrespectful.
Breaking directions into discrete, visually postable steps prevents students from mentally 'moving on' before instructions finish.
Checking for understanding and pausing before the 'go' signal shifts responsibility for success onto students.
Once directions have been properly given, further breakdowns are an execution problem to be corrected with 'do it again,' not repeated instruction.
quotes: The reason your students don’t follow directions well is because they mentally move on before you finish giving them. Once they think they know what you’re asking of them, they’re gone.
Repeating directions for your students and answering questions that have already been answered wastes boatloads of time and is incredibly frustrating. But it’s easily correctable.

Just before giving your “go” signal, ask if there is anyone who doesn’t know exactly what to do. This is an effective questioning technique that shifts the burden of responsibility from you and your instruction, to your students and their execution.

It’s important to note, however, that you shouldn’t have to repeat your directions. At this point, if you’ve followed the steps above, it’s an execution problem. The responsibility now lies solely with your students.
Do this and follow the nine steps, and their best is what you’ll get.
